items.meaning: Central Processing Unit: a component that executes program instructions.
items.use: The anchor term for every element.

items.meaning: Control unit (decodes instructions and sends the control signals that coordinate the fetch-decode-execute cycle; it does not execute them itself), ALU, registers (program counter PC, memory address register MAR, memory data register MDR, current instruction register CIR, accumulator ACC), cache, buses and clock.
items.use: Describe features and trace the cycle.

items.meaning: The repeated cycle: the PC gives the address, the instruction passes through the MAR, MDR and CIR, is decoded and executed, and results go to the accumulator. The PC then moves on.
items.use: Explain the process and trace programs.

items.meaning: Clock pulses per second, in hertz (Hz). 1 GHz = one billion cycles per second = 1,000,000,000 Hz; CPUs today commonly run at 3 to 5 GHz (1980s: 3 to 5 MHz). A cycle is not a completed instruction.
Clock speed, cache size (multi-level L1, L2, L3), number of cores and memory. Cores each run their own instructions but can wait for each other; overclocking raises speed but also power use and heat.
A processor with many simpler cores for parallel tasks.

checks: What are the three stages of the cycle?
How many Hz are in 1 GHz?
Name three factors that affect performance.
recall.bridge: Explain how a larger cache improves performance.

quote.text: Careful that the purpose is not an action such as fetches, takes, retrieves.

units: decodes instructions and sends control signals that coordinate the other parts
tiny, fast stores inside the CPU

worked.text:
Control unit: decodes instructions and sends control signals that coordinate the other parts.
ALU: performs arithmetic and logical operations.
Registers: tiny, fast stores inside the CPU; the PC holds the address of the next instruction to be fetched.
Cache: fast memory close to the processor, for frequently used data and instructions.
Clock: provides timing signals that keep the CPU's operations in step.

A.answer: The CPU has a hard drive and RAM.
A.feedback: “Take one component. What does it do while a program runs?” If that is not enough: “The PC holds an address. The address of what?” Then withdraw the hint and ask for the full description of each component.

B.answer:
Control unit: decodes instructions and sends control signals.
ALU: the brain of the CPU.
Registers: store data.
Cache: stores data.
Clock: controls the speed of the computer.
B.why: Only the control unit has its exact purpose. “Stores data” could be any memory, so it says nothing about registers or cache; the ALU as “the brain” is a label; and the clock sends timing signals, it does not “control the speed”.
B.feedback: “What exactly does it hold or do? Say it without a label.”

C.feedback: A fresh, independent task: “Describe the main parts of a computer around the CPU: main memory, secondary storage, input and output.”

pattern.when: Divide the marks by the number of things asked for
pattern.earns: 1 mark per thing: state each point. 2 marks per thing: a point and its expansion.
Mark 1: the point. Mark 2: how it works or why it helps.
pattern.example: AQA 8525/2, June 2022, Q15.2, a security measure beyond a password: a code sent to a phone (1); a hacker would also need the phone (1).

pattern.earns: Three points; or a name (1) and two points describing it; or three steps in order.
pattern.example: AQA 8525/2, June 2023, Q8.2, the role of the clock, control unit and a register: 1 mark for each component. OCR J277/01, June 2023, Q4(b), name and describe one threat: the threat (1), what it does (1) … and what it achieves (1).

pattern.earns: Each benefit (1) and its application to the scenario (1).
pattern.example: OCR J277/01, June 2024, Q2(b)(i), wired network at an airport: fast connection (1) so check-in is not delayed (1). The same 2 + 2 shape for “one benefit and one drawback”.

pattern.earns: 1 mark per difference. Each must say both sides.
pattern.example: AQA 8525/2, June 2022, Q14.2: a LAN covers a small area, a WAN a wide one (1).

pattern.when: Describe the steps or the process
pattern.earns: 1 mark per step, in order and precise.
pattern.example: OCR J277/02, June 2022, Q3(c), linear search: start at the first value (1); check every value in order (1). “One by one” alone is not enough.

rejects: Steps that miss one of the ideas the mark needs.
marks.example: AQA 8525/2, June 2023, Q8.2: describe the role of the clock, control unit and a register
marks.weak: Vague roles: the control unit “controls the computer”; a register is “fast memory”, with no word on what it holds.
marks.strong: Gives each component its specific job, such as a register holding the address of the next instruction.
marks.marking: One mark for each relevant point. A few also credit an expansion of a point.

roadmap.framing: From what assessments require, through what materials explicitly teach, to what students can construct independently.
roadmap.question: In three education systems (England, Singapore and China), which relationships do comparable computing exam questions require students to express; how explicitly do each system’s curriculum documents and teaching materials teach those relationships; and can students construct them unaided on matched tasks?
roadmap.purpose: It tests where answer-building is made visible, rather than assuming high-performing systems already do it better.

stages.label: Required linkage
stages.question: What relationships must the answer express?
stages.evidence: Exam papers and mark schemes, each question part coded for the relationship it requires.
stages.now: Started: UK papers with full mark schemes; Singapore specimen papers marked by borrowed Cambridge schemes; one Zhejiang paper with reference answers from a resource site. Enough to explore, not yet to establish differences between systems.

stages.label: Taught linkage
stages.question: How do teaching materials make constructing those relationships explicit?
stages.evidence: Specifications, syllabuses, textbooks and classroom materials for matched topics and tasks, read against one checklist.
stages.now: Not started. The crucial next step for the argument.

stages.label: Independent linkage
stages.question: Can students construct them without support, including later and on a different task?
stages.evidence: Students’ answers to matched tasks, recorded on the missing-link ladder: unaided, after a prompt, a hint or the model, and on a new task later.
stages.now: Not started: needs the student study in each system.

checklist: Labels the purpose of each answer element.
Models decisions about selecting and connecting knowledge.
Provides practice with progressively less support.
roadmap.rule: Where a feature is absent, record “not found in the sampled materials”, never that a country does not teach it.
roadmap.comparable: Comparable means the same topic, the same command word and the same level, as with Describe on all three ladders.
